To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the polarization from density (scalar) perturbations is the same (in the sense of amplitude) in any model that fits the BBN baryon density, the degree-scale anisotropic measurements, and the polarization from gravitational waves (the tensor modes) is the same (again in the sense of amplitude).

the polarization of the CMB is detectable in a survey of a few hundred square degrees with an angular resolution of a degree and a sensitivity of a few microkelvins, and that a survey of a smaller area of sky with a deeper sensitivity is preferable to a larger survey with a shallower sensitivity.

the amplitude (detectability) of the CMB polarization from scalar modes is roughly constant in all inflationary models, that the amplitude (dectectability) of the tensor modes is proportional to the tensor-to-scalar ratio r (and thus is smaller than the scalar modes), and that the sensitivity of the polarization measurement is improved in fixed-time experiments with deeper surveys of smaller areas of sky.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the polarization of the CMB is detectable in the next generation of experiments.

a polarization experiment with an angular resolution of a few degrees and sensitivity to the polarization on degree scales of 1 part in 10 ^{3} (or less) is capable of detecting the polarization from density fluctuations and gravitational waves.
the detectability of both the density perturbation and gravitational wave polarization is a strong function of the survey area and the sensitivity of the experiment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the detectability of polarization is not very dependent on the underlying cosmological model as long as it is consistent with the BBN baryon density, and the angular resolution is better than 1°.
the detectability of both the scalar and tensor modes depends on the sky coverage, resolution, and sensitivity of the experiment.
the polarization of the CMB is detectable if the experiment covers 10% of the sky, has an angular resolution of 10' or better, and has a sensitivity to temperature anisotropies of 1 mu K or better.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the polarization of the CMB is a powerful probe of cosmological physics, and that the sensitivity of an experiment is a strong function of the angular resolution and sky coverage.
the polarization of the CMB is an excellent probe of the physics of the early universe and that it is possible to measure this polarization with current and next-generation experiments.
polarization measurements are not a panacea for cosmology.
